title: Photos synced as base64 into Postgres; Storage uploader orphaned
problem: compressImage returns base64 data-URLs stored in formData.photos; syncAll pushes them verbatim via mapMemoryToSupabase into memories.photos (upsert 245). photoStorageService.ensureRemotePhotoUrls is never called in src (dead in main), so each photo is a multi-MB base64 string in a Postgres row, causing row bloat, large egress (SELECT 330 fetches photos) and likely upsert failures. Violates CLAUDE.md 2.16.
fix: In syncAll, before upsert/update, call ensureRemotePhotoUrls to upload local photos, swap base64 for URLs, persist to Dexie, then upsert URLs.

verdict.reasoning:
The finding is accurate on every load-bearing point.

1. compressImage (src/utils/imageUtils.ts:41) resolves via reader.readAsDataURL(blob) — it returns a base64 data: URL, not a Storage URL. Confirmed at lines 75/77.

2. MemoryForm.handlePhotoUpload (src/components/MemoryForm.tsx:614-617) pushes that base64 string verbatim into formData.photos. On save (lines 504 & 521) formData.photos is passed straight into memoryService.create/update, with no upload step.

3. memoryService stores it in Dexie and queues a sync. In syncAll, mapMemoryToSupabase (memoryService.ts:21) copies photos verbatim, and the create path upserts supabaseData into memories (line 245) while the update path forwards updates.photos verbatim (line 270). The DB column memories.photos is text[] (migration 20251220174815_remote_schema.sql:96), so each photo becomes a multi-MB base64 text-array element in a Postgres row.

4. ensureRemotePhotoUrls (photoStorageService.ts:43) is genuinely dead in the main src/ tree — Grep shows the only callers are inside .claude/worktrees/tender-lederberg/ (a separate worktree, not the main branch). So the Storage uploader is orphaned exactly as claimed.

5. The egress concern is real: the incremental pull query (memoryService.ts:330) explicitly SELECTs the photos column, so every sync re-downloads the base64 blobs. Row bloat + large egress + risk of upsert payload-size failures all follow. This violates CLAUDE.md 2.16 (photos must go through photoStorageService, must be compressed/uploaded, not stored inline).

The proposed fix (call ensureRemotePhotoUrls in syncAll before upsert/update, swap base64 for URLs, persist URLs to Dexie, then push URLs) is the correct direction. The maintainers already prototyped exactly this in the tender-lederberg worktree, and that prototype is more robust than the one-line proposal: it only uploads when photos.some(isLocalPhotoRef), persists the returned URLs back to db.memories, and wraps the upload in try/catch so a failed upload doesn't permanently block the memory's sync.

Caveats the bare proposal omits (why fixSafe is qualified): (a) There is NO migration or config.toml entry creating the memory-photos Storage bucket or its RLS/Storage policies — config.toml:109 has the buckets section commented out and no migration touches storage.objects. The bucket presumably exists only in the remote project dashboard (ADD_MEMORY_QA.md:88 flags it as a prerequisite). If the bucket/policies are absent in any environment, every upload throws and the worktree fallback sets photos:[] — silently dropping photos from the cloud (they survive locally in Dexie). Any merge of this fix must verify the bucket + Storage policies exist. (b) The worktree version uses bare console.warn, which violates CLAUDE.md 1.15 — it should be guarded behind import.meta.env.DEV like the rest of memoryService, or routed through errorLoggingService. (c) Failed-upload fallback behavior (sync memory without photos vs. defer the whole item for retry) is a product decision worth making explicit rather than silently dropping.
verdict.refinedFix:
Wire ensureRemotePhotoUrls into syncAll, mirroring the tender-lederberg worktree but tightening the gaps:

CREATE path (memoryService.ts, before the upsert at line 245):
  const supabaseData = mapMemoryToSupabase(memory)
  if (supabaseData.photos.length > 0 && supabaseData.photos.some(isLocalPhotoRef)) {
    const remoteUrls = await photoStorageService.ensureRemotePhotoUrls({ userId, memoryId: memory.id, photos: supabaseData.photos })
    supabaseData.photos = remoteUrls
    await db.memories.update(memory.id, { photos: remoteUrls })   // persist URLs so re-sync/pull doesn't re-upload
  }

UPDATE path (around line 270): same guard on updates.photos before assigning supabaseUpdates.photos; on success write remoteUrls back to db.memories.update(id, { photos: remoteUrls }).

Differences from the worktree prototype (apply these):
- Do NOT swallow upload errors with bare console.warn. Either (preferred) let the upload error propagate so the existing catch (line 301) marks the item failed and retries with backoff — keeping photos local until upload succeeds rather than silently writing photos:[] to the cloud; or if you intentionally want best-effort, log via errorLoggingService and guard any console.warn behind import.meta.env.DEV (CLAUDE.md 1.15). Letting it retry is safer for data integrity.
- Import isLocalPhotoRef and photoStorageService at top of memoryService.ts.

Prerequisite (must verify before shipping, not part of the code change): confirm the memory-photos Storage bucket exists in every Supabase environment with RLS/Storage policies scoped to the path prefix `${userId}/...`. There is currently no migration creating it (config.toml:109 buckets are commented out). If absent, add a Storage bucket + policy migration so uploads succeed; otherwise the fix degrades to dropping cloud photos.

A one-time backfill for existing rows that already contain base64 in memories.photos is out of scope for this change but should be tracked separately.

title: Conflict UI dead; sync never sets conflict fields (silent data loss)
problem: Home renders ConflictResolutionDialog on m.conflict && m.conflictCloud but nothing sets them. Pull-sync (350-357) is last-write-wins; an offline edit on A while B pushed a newer cloud change skips the cloud branch and A later overwrites it, losing B's edit with no dialog.
fix: When existing && !existing.synced && cloudTime>localTime and content differs, set conflict/conflictCloud/conflictDetectedAt so the dialog resolves it; else remove the dead UI.

verdict.reasoning:
The CORE of the finding is CONFIRMED and real. I grep'd the entire src tree: the conflict fields (conflict/conflictCloud/conflictDetectedAt) are ONLY ever assigned in ConflictResolutionDialog.tsx, and there they are only ever CLEARED (set to false/undefined, lines 39-41, 58-60). Nothing — not memoryService.syncAll, not the mappers, not any service — ever sets conflict:true or assigns a conflictCloud Memory. So Home.tsx's detection (line 107: `memories.find(m => m.conflict && m.conflictCloud)`) can never match, the dialog rendered at Home.tsx:925-934 is dead code, and the full dialog + both tr/en i18n keys (i18n.ts:1088-1096, 2161-2169) exist but are unreachable.

The data-loss mechanism is also real, and is actually WORSE/different from how the finding frames it. memoryService.ts pull branch (lines 350-357) overwrites local only when `cloudTime > localTime && existing.synced`. The `existing.synced` guard means an unsynced offline edit is NEVER replaced by a newer cloud row during pull — the cloud edit is silently skipped. Then the local edit is pushed to cloud via the queue at lines 279-283 with `.update(supabaseUpdates).eq('id', id)` — field-level last-write-wins, NO updated_at precondition — clobbering device B's newer edit. No conflict is ever surfaced. So device B's edit is lost silently. Confirmed high-impact silent data loss for multi-device users.

WHY PARTIAL, not confirmed: the proposed fix is placed on the WRONG branch and would frequently fail to fire. In syncAll the PUSH loop (lines 229-314) runs strictly BEFORE the PULL loop (lines 319+). In the normal online path, A's queued edit is pushed to cloud first (succeeds, then `db.memories.update(id,{synced:true})` at line 286). By the time the pull reaches lines 350-357, existing.synced is already true, so the proposed `!existing.synced` condition is false — the fix never triggers and B's edit is already gone. The proposed pull-branch fix only catches the conflict in the narrow case where A's push failed or hadn't run yet. To actually prevent the loss, detection must happen before the push overwrites cloud: either reorder so reconciliation/pull runs before push, OR (cleaner) add optimistic-concurrency to the push update (`.eq('id',id).eq('updated_at', existing.updatedAt)` or `.gt`-style guard); when the conditional update affects 0 rows, fetch the cloud row and set the conflict fields so the now-live dialog resolves it. The finding's severity (high) is correct; the proposed fix's direction (wire up the dialog by setting conflict fields when cloud is newer than an unsynced local edit) is correct, but the specific placement/condition is unsafe-incomplete and would leave the data-loss window mostly open.
verdict.refinedFix: Detect the conflict BEFORE the push clobbers cloud, using optimistic concurrency on the push. In memoryService.syncAll, for the 'update' op (around lines 279-286): change the Supabase update to a conditional update guarded by the last-known cloud updated_at, e.g. fetch the current cloud updated_at first (or include `.eq('updated_at', existingCloudUpdatedAt)`), and check the affected row count. If the guarded update affects 0 rows, the cloud row changed underneath us: SELECT the current cloud row, map it with mapSupabaseToMemory, and write conflict fields onto the local memory via `db.memories.update(id, { conflict: true, conflictCloud: cloudMemory, conflictDetectedAt: new Date().toISOString() })`, then mark the queue item done (do NOT overwrite cloud). Leave the existing pull branch (350-357) as-is; the now-populated conflict fields make Home.tsx's dialog appear, and ConflictResolutionDialog already resolves it correctly (keepLocal re-queues a sync; keepCloud copies cloud into local). This closes the loss window because the conflict is detected at push time, before any overwrite. Alternative if optimistic concurrency is too invasive: reorder syncAll so the pull/reconciliation runs first and, in the pull branch, when `existing && !existing.synced && cloudTime > localTime` and content differs, set the conflict fields and SKIP queuing the push until resolved — but this requires also gating the push loop on the conflict flag so it doesn't immediately overwrite. The bare proposed fix (only adding the condition to the pull branch) is not sufficient because push runs first. Confirm npm run build passes; no i18n changes needed (keys already exist in tr+en).

title: Streak day-delta uses UTC-parsed dates vs local today (off-by-one)
problem: new Date('YYYY-MM-DD') is UTC midnight, then setHours snaps to local midnight of the local day it falls on. In UTC-negative zones a memory dated today reads as the prior day; verified daysSinceEnd=1 for today, so gap math (46) and active check (71-73) are off by one and streaks reset a day early.
fix: Parse locally: const [y,mo,d]=str.split('-').map(Number); new Date(y,mo-1,d). Apply to prev, curr, lastStreakEnd, lastMemoryDate.

title: Badge unlockedAt uses positional index on unsorted memories
problem: Reads memories[0/9/49].createdAt, but getAll returns Dexie UUID-pkey order, not createdAt, so the unlock date is arbitrary and changes on re-sync.
fix: Sort a copy by createdAt asc and use byCreated[0/9/49]; same for intensity badge find.

title: Statistics counters produce NaN on out-of-enum values
problem: categoryCount[m.category]++ on a value outside the hardcoded record is undefined++ = NaN, breaking a chart segment.
fix: Guard with if(m.category in categoryCount), init missing keys to 0, or bucket unknown into uncategorized.

title: Daily full-sync deletion can race an in-flight create
problem: Reconciliation deletes local memories absent from a single allRemote id snapshot; a create upserted by another device/tab or not yet visible due to replication is wrongly treated as remotely-deleted and removed.
fix: Re-verify the id via select('id').eq('id',local.id) before deleting, or only delete memories older than the snapshot time.

title: users table allows clients to self-grant premium / unlimited Aiya messages (column-level authz gap)
problem: The RLS UPDATE policy on public.users is `CREATE POLICY "Users can update own data" ON users FOR UPDATE USING (auth.uid() = id)` with no WITH CHECK and no column-level restriction. The client writes to the users table directly (EditProfileSheet.tsx:125 supabase.from('users').update(updates).eq('id', user.id); userService.ts:94/114). Because PostgREST exposes the table and the policy permits updating ANY column of one's own row, an authenticated user can open the devtools console and run supabase.from('users').update({ is_premium: true, aiya_messages_limit: 9999999 }).eq('id', myId). This bypasses the entire Aiya paywall and usage metering that the aiya-chat edge function enforces via aiya_messages_used >= aiya_messages_limit (functions/aiya-chat/index.ts:213). It directly translates to uncapped OpenAI spend on the project's key.
fix: Move billing/usage columns out of client write reach. Either (a) REVOKE UPDATE on the sensitive columns from the authenticated role and only let the service-role edge function modify them: `REVOKE UPDATE (is_premium, aiya_messages_used, aiya_messages_limit) ON public.users FROM authenticated;` plus a column GRANT for the editable profile columns; or (b) replace the broad UPDATE policy with a trigger/check that rejects changes to is_premium/aiya_messages_limit/aiya_messages_used unless the request comes from service_role. Keep the edge function (service-role) as the only writer of usage/premium fields.

verdict.reasoning: Verified against actual code. (1) RLS policy at supabase/migrations/20251220174815_remote_schema.sql:247 is `CREATE POLICY "Users can update own data" ON users FOR UPDATE USING (auth.uid() = id)` — no WITH CHECK, no column restriction. (2) Lines 485-487 grant `GRANT ALL ON TABLE public.users TO authenticated`, so PostgREST exposes column-level UPDATE on every column to the authenticated role. (3) Sensitive billing columns is_premium (line 111), aiya_messages_used (112), aiya_messages_limit (113) live on this same row. (4) The client writes directly to the table: EditProfileSheet.tsx:125 (`supabase.from('users').update(updates).eq('id', user.id)`) and userService.ts:94/114 use the anon/auth client. Nothing stops an authenticated user from opening devtools and running `supabase.from('users').update({ is_premium: true, aiya_messages_limit: 9999999 }).eq('id', myId)`. (5) The paywall depends entirely on these columns: aiya-chat/index.ts:213 returns 429 when `usageUsed >= usageLimit`, reading aiya_messages_used/aiya_messages_limit at lines 176/209. So self-granting a huge limit (or flipping is_premium) defeats metering → uncapped OpenAI spend on the project key. The exploit is real and the severity is correctly high. CRUCIAL for fix safety: every write that increments aiya_messages_used and the row-creation upsert in the edge function use supabaseAdmin (SERVICE_ROLE_KEY) — lines 168, 187, 366-371, 463, 494. service_role bypasses RLS and is unaffected by column REVOKEs on the authenticated role, so removing authenticated's UPDATE on those three columns does NOT break metering, premium provisioning, or row creation. One nuance the original fix missed: the editable profile columns (display_name, bio, avatar_url, birthday, location) are NOT in the base migration's users table (lines 108-121); they are added later by 20260206050000_add_profile_fields.sql. Any explicit column re-GRANT must list the full editable set or it will break profile edits. The cleanest, lowest-risk form is a column-level REVOKE of just the three sensitive columns from the table-wide GRANT ALL (which leaves all other columns writable), rather than revoking all and re-granting a hand-maintained list that can drift as columns are added.
verdict.refinedFix:
Use a column-level REVOKE (option a), not a full revoke-and-re-grant, to avoid breaking profile edits when new columns are added. New migration supabase/migrations/<timestamp>_lock_users_billing_columns.sql:

-- Remove client (authenticated/anon) ability to write billing/usage columns.
-- service_role bypasses RLS/grants, so the aiya-chat edge function (which uses
-- SERVICE_ROLE_KEY) remains the sole writer of these fields. All other user
-- columns stay client-writable, so EditProfileSheet profile saves keep working.
REVOKE UPDATE (is_premium, aiya_messages_used, aiya_messages_limit) ON public.users FROM authenticated;
REVOKE UPDATE (is_premium, aiya_messages_used, aiya_messages_limit) ON public.users FROM anon;

-- Harden the row-ownership check on UPDATE (original policy had USING only).
-- WITH CHECK prevents a user from re-pointing their row's id to another user.
DROP POLICY IF EXISTS "Users can update own data" ON public.users;
CREATE POLICY "Users can update own data" ON public.users
  FOR UPDATE
  USING (auth.uid() = id)
  WITH CHECK (auth.uid() = id);

Notes: (1) A column-level REVOKE narrows the pre-existing table-wide GRANT ALL — Postgres column privileges are intersected with table privileges, so this is sufficient; no need to enumerate the editable columns. (2) Verify no other authenticated-client code path writes these three columns. userService.ts:114 upsert sets is_premium/aiya_messages_used/aiya_messages_limit on INSERT (new-row creation) — a column-level UPDATE revoke does NOT block INSERT, so first-time row creation via the client still works; however if you also want to stop clients from seeding is_premium=true on insert, add `REVOKE INSERT (is_premium, aiya_messages_used, aiya_messages_limit) ...` too. Defaults (false/0/30) cover the columns when omitted. (3) Test after applying: profile edit (display_name/bio/avatar/birthday/location) must still succeed for authenticated users; a direct client update of is_premium/aiya_messages_limit must now fail; and an Aiya message must still increment usage via the edge function.

title: daily_question_answers exposes private journaling answers via user-controlled is_public flag
problem: daily_question_answers has policy `CREATE POLICY "Anyone can read public answers" ON daily_question_answers FOR SELECT USING (is_public = true)`. The INSERT policy only checks WITH CHECK (auth.uid() = user_id) and does not constrain is_public, so a user (or the app on their behalf) can insert rows with is_public=true, and there is no UPDATE policy restricting toggling is_public. Any anonymous/anon-role caller can then SELECT every answer marked public — these are personal journal answers (answer_text) tied to a user_id. For a private memory-journaling app this is a meaningful data-exposure path that ships enabled even though no UI surfaces a 'make public' control yet.
fix: Until a vetted public-sharing feature exists, drop the `Anyone can read public answers` policy (so answers are strictly owner-readable). If public answers are a real product requirement, gate the SELECT on an explicitly anonymized/curated view rather than exposing raw answer_text+user_id, and add a guard so is_public can only be set through a reviewed server path.

verdict.reasoning: Re-read supabase/migrations/20260206100000_memory_system_overhaul.sql in full. Confirmed: (1) Lines 111-113 define policy "Anyone can read public answers" ON daily_question_answers FOR SELECT USING (is_public = true) with NO role restriction. (2) Lines 160-162 GRANT ALL on the table TO anon/authenticated/service_role. Because RLS permissive policies are OR-combined and this one is not role-scoped, ANY caller using the public anon key (shipped in every PWA/Android client) can run SELECT * FROM daily_question_answers WHERE is_public = true and read answer_text + user_id — personal journal answers. That exposure path is real. (3) Lines 106-108 INSERT policy WITH CHECK (auth.uid() = user_id) does NOT constrain is_public, so a user crafting a raw request (bypassing the app) can insert their OWN rows with is_public=true. The app itself (src/services/dailyQuestionService.ts:160) always inserts is_public:false and no UI surfaces a 'make public' control. TWO corrections to the finding: (a) The finding implies a missing UPDATE policy lets users 'toggle' is_public — but under Postgres RLS, the ABSENCE of an UPDATE policy means UPDATE is DENIED entirely (I grepped all migrations; there is no FOR UPDATE policy on this table). So toggling existing rows is NOT a vector; the only write vector is at INSERT time, and it only lets a user expose their own data. (b) The INSERT vector is self-exposure only — a user cannot mark other users' rows public (WITH CHECK enforces auth.uid()=user_id). The cross-user leak only materializes once any public rows exist, and today none do because the app hardcodes false. So this is a latent ship-disabled misconfiguration, not an active mass data leak — which warrants medium, not high.
verdict.refinedFix: Drop the unvetted public-read policy in a new migration (filename format YYYYMMDDHHMMSS_*.sql per CLAUDE.md rule 2.2): `DROP POLICY IF EXISTS "Anyone can read public answers" ON public.daily_question_answers;`. This is safe and non-breaking: the app only ever reads via the owner policy "Users can read own answers" (auth.uid() = user_id) and always inserts is_public=false (src/services/dailyQuestionService.ts:160), so no current code path depends on the public policy. After dropping it, answers become strictly owner-readable. Optionally also harden the INSERT path so future code can't accidentally create public rows: replace the INSERT policy WITH CHECK with `(auth.uid() = user_id AND is_public = false)`, or revoke the column-level INSERT/UPDATE on is_public from anon/authenticated. If public sharing later becomes a real product requirement, expose it through a curated/anonymized VIEW (omitting user_id, with vetted answer_text) and gate is_public mutation behind a SECURITY DEFINER server function rather than re-adding a raw table-level USING (is_public = true) policy. Note: the finding's 'toggle via missing UPDATE policy' rationale is inaccurate — no UPDATE policy means UPDATE is already blocked; the real vector is INSERT-time self-exposure.

title: Aiya usage metering is client-controlled via countUsage flag
problem: The edge function only increments aiya_messages_used when the request body's countUsage !== false (index.ts:365, 460, 491). The flag comes straight from the client payload (aiyaService passes countUsage: true for chat/analysis but false for classify/category). A user can call the function directly with countUsage:false on the 'chat' action and run unlimited paid gpt-4o completions without the counter ever advancing, defeating the 50-message limit and OpenAI cost controls.
fix: Determine whether usage should be counted on the server based on action, not on a client-supplied flag — e.g. always count for 'chat'/'analysis'/'profile' and never for 'classify'/'category', ignoring any client countUsage value. Remove countUsage from the trusted request contract.

title: No server-side rate limiting on the OpenAI cost path; rate limiter is client-side in-memory only
problem: rateLimiter is a per-tab in-memory Map (rateLimiter.ts:11-50) and is only ever used for photo uploads (photoStorageService.ts:53). It is trivially bypassed (refresh, new tab, or direct API call) and is not applied to the Aiya/OpenAI path at all. The only server-side throttle is the cumulative 50-message lifetime-ish counter in the edge function; there is no per-minute/burst limit, so an authenticated user (within their remaining quota, or after raising the limit per security-1) can hammer gpt-4o concurrently. Combined with the large max_tokens (CHAT_MAX_TOKENS=2000) this is a real cost/abuse exposure.
fix: Add a server-side per-user burst limit in the edge function (e.g. a short-window counter in a Postgres table or KV keyed by userId) before calling OpenAI, returning 429 when exceeded. Treat the client rateLimiter only as UX, not a security control.

title: Edge function CORS allows any origin with Access-Control-Allow-Origin: '*'
problem: corsHeaders sets 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin': '*' (index.ts:5). The function does require a valid Bearer JWT, so '*' is not catastrophic, but it lets any website invoke the function with a victim's leaked/forwarded token and incurs OpenAI cost against this project, and removes origin as a defense layer for a production app that has a known web origin and Capacitor scheme.
fix: Restrict the allowed origin to the app's known web origin(s) and the Capacitor scheme (e.g. reflect the request Origin only if it is in an allowlist, otherwise omit the header). Keep Vary: Origin.

title: Documented Content-Security-Policy is never actually applied
problem: CSP_CONFIGURATION.md specifies a full CSP (connect-src limited to supabase + api.openai.com, object-src none, frame-ancestors none, etc.), but index.html contains no Content-Security-Policy <meta http-equiv> tag and there is no host-level header config in the repo. So the documented CSP provides zero runtime protection for the deployed PWA; any injected script could exfiltrate the user's Supabase session token from localStorage to an arbitrary endpoint.
fix: Add the CSP as a <meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy"> tag in index.html (or, preferably, as a real response header on the hosting platform) matching CSP_CONFIGURATION.md, and verify nothing breaks (the doc already accounts for supabase/openai connect-src).

title: users INSERT RLS policy uses WITH CHECK (true), allowing rows for arbitrary ids
problem: `CREATE POLICY "Users can insert own data" ON users FOR INSERT WITH CHECK (true)` permits any authenticated caller to insert a users row with ANY id value (not constrained to auth.uid()). The FK to auth.users(id) limits ids to real auth users, but a caller can still pre-create/seed a row for another existing auth user id (e.g. set their email/profile fields, or pre-seed is_premium=false to interfere), since nothing ties the inserted id to the caller.
fix: Tighten to `WITH CHECK (auth.uid() = id)`. The legitimate self-provisioning paths (userService.ensureUserExists, Login.tsx upsert) already insert id = the current user's id, so this should not break them; the edge function uses the service role and bypasses RLS.

title: Memory photos stored in a public-read bucket with no Storage RLS in repo
problem: Photos are uploaded to bucket 'memory-photos' and surfaced via getPublicUrl (photoStorageService.ts:100), meaning the bucket is public-read: anyone holding a URL can fetch a user's private journal photo with no authentication or expiry. Paths use random UUIDs (userId/memoryId/uuid.ext, line 75) so they are not trivially enumerable, but public URLs leak via referrers/sharing/CDN logs and there are no Storage RLS policies committed in supabase/migrations to scope reads to the owner. For a private journaling app, image privacy depends entirely on URL secrecy.
fix: Make the bucket private and serve images via createSignedUrl (short-lived) instead of getPublicUrl, with Storage RLS policies restricting object access to auth.uid() = (storage.foldername(name))[1]. If signed URLs are too heavy for the UX, at minimum commit the storage policies and document the public-bucket tradeoff explicitly.

title: Crisis tier detected but no safety instructions ever reach the model — no escalation, no hotline
problem: routeMessage() classifies messages containing CRISIS_WORDS (intihar/suicide/'ölmek istiyorum'/'kill myself' etc.) as tier 'crisis', but the ONLY effect is loading more memories/history/profile — the tier is never passed to the edge function and never changes the prompt. handleSend selects systemPromptFull (the same generic companion prompt) for crisis, and that prompt (src/i18n.ts:525-961) contains ZERO crisis/safety guidance. Worse, it explicitly bans the exact supportive register a crisis needs: it forbids 'buradayım/güvenli alan' (BÖLÜM 2, line 585), forbids saying it's an AI, and declares 'Sen bir terapi botu DEGILSIN' (line 535). So a user expressing suicidal intent receives a casual, opinionated 'friend' response with no professional-help referral, no hotline, no de-escalation. This is the highest-risk gap in the product.
fix: Pass route.tier (or a crisis flag) into aiyaService.sendMessage and into the edge function payload. In supabase/functions/aiya-chat/index.ts, when crisis is flagged, prepend a hard safety system message that overrides the companion persona: validate feelings, express care plainly, and surface region-appropriate crisis resources (e.g. Türkiye 182 / international hotlines) and urge contacting a professional or emergency services. Add a crisis section to the i18n prompt (tr+en) that is injected only for the crisis tier. Keep CRISIS_WORDS detection but also handle the messageCountInChat===0 case so a first-message crisis still escalates (currently first message returns tier 'deep', bypassing the crisis branch — see ai-aiya-4).

verdict.reasoning:
All factual claims verified against the actual code.

1. routeMessage() (aiyaService.ts:91-117): CRISIS_WORDS (intihar/suicide/'ölmek istiyorum'/'kill myself' etc., lines 68-72) DO trigger tier 'crisis' at lines 100-103, but the RouteResult only carries memoryCount/historyLimit/includeStats/includeFullPrompt/includeProfile. The `tier` string itself is never consumed to alter the prompt or payload — confirmed.

2. handleSend (Aiya.tsx:895-919): for crisis, includeFullPrompt=true and includeProfile=true so selectedPrompt = systemPromptFull (the generic companion prompt). aiyaService.sendMessage is called with only {message, history, memories, locale, systemPrompt, memoryContext}. route.tier is NOT passed — confirmed.

3. sendMessage signature (aiyaService.ts:536-555) and the edge function AiyaRequest type (index.ts:48-56) have NO tier/crisis field. The chat branch (index.ts:476-504) builds `system` via normalizeSystemPrompt and forwards to OpenAI with zero crisis handling — confirmed.

4. I read the ENTIRE aiyaSystemPrompt (i18n.ts:525-961). It contains zero crisis/suicide/hotline/emergency/de-escalation guidance. It explicitly says 'Sen bir terapi botu DEGILSIN' (line 535), forbids 'Yapay zeka olarak / Ben bir AI' (line 588), and forbids constantly using 'buradayim / paylasabilirsin / guvenli alan' (line 585). (Minor nuance: line 937 uses 'buradayim' as an allowed example for heavy moments, so the supportive register is discouraged, not 100% banned — but no professional-referral/hotline content exists at all.) Confirmed.

5. First-message bypass: routeMessage returns tier 'deep' for messageCountInChat===0 at lines 96-98, which executes BEFORE the crisis check at line 101. So a first-message crisis is classified 'deep'. Today this is functionally harmless because both 'deep'-first-message and 'crisis' load the identical full prompt with no crisis content — but if crisis escalation is later gated on tier==='crisis', the first message would silently bypass it. The cross-reference to ai-aiya-4 is accurate.

Tempering factors (not disproving the finding): GPT-4o has its own safety training that typically surfaces crisis resources regardless of system prompt, and the persona's 'KULLANICI UZGUN' / 'SESSIZLIGIN GUCU' sections push listening/empathy for heavy disclosures. So the gap is 'no app-level safety guarantee, no localized hotline (182), persona register works against ideal crisis response' rather than 'guaranteed harmful output'. Given this is a production journaling app prepping for Play Store launch in a mental-health-adjacent domain, the gap is still serious.
verdict.refinedFix:
The fix direction is correct and non-breaking (all additions are optional params / optional prompt section). Concrete safe implementation:

1. Edge function (supabase/functions/aiya-chat/index.ts): add optional `crisis?: boolean` to AiyaRequest (index.ts:48-56). In the chat branch (around line 477), when `crisis === true`, push an ADDITIONAL high-priority system message BEFORE the persona system message rather than mutating/replacing it: e.g. messages = [{role:'system', content: CRISIS_SAFETY_PROMPT}, ...(system ? [{role:'system', content: system}] : []), ...history, {role:'user', content: message}]. The crisis prompt must: validate feelings plainly, drop the 'not an AI / no buradayim' persona constraints, express care, urge contacting a professional/emergency services, and surface region-appropriate resources (Türkiye: 182; for international users an appropriate hotline). Localize via locale (tr/en). Keep persona override explicit so the safety message wins.

2. Client: add optional `crisis?: boolean` to aiyaService.sendMessage params (aiyaService.ts:536) and forward it in invokeAiya payload — additive, no existing call sites break. In Aiya.tsx handleSend, pass `crisis: route.tier === 'crisis'`.

3. i18n.ts: add aiyaCrisisPrompt (or pass the crisis copy from edge constant) with BOTH tr and en, per CLAUDE.md i18n rule. If the safety copy lives client-side it must be in i18n; if it lives in the edge function it should be a constant keyed by locale.

4. First-message ordering: move the crisis check ABOVE the messageCountInChat===0 early-return in routeMessage (currently lines 96-103) so a first-message crisis is classified 'crisis', not 'deep'. Reorder: crisis check first, then the messageCountInChat===0 deep default. This is required for the crisis flag to fire on a first message.

5. Detection caveat (not blocking, worth noting): CRISIS_WORDS is a substring match on lowercased text and will miss negations/paraphrases and produce occasional false positives — acceptable for a safety net that only ADDS resources, but do not gate any feature-removal on it.

Risk note: do NOT remove the persona prompt entirely for crisis (that would be a behavior regression for borderline false-positive matches); layering an overriding safety system message is the safe approach. Also verify token budget — prepending the crisis block alongside the full persona prompt is fine within gpt-4o context, but the crisis prompt should be concise.

title: Usage accounting is non-atomic read-then-write — concurrent requests double-count, users exceed limit / cost leaks
problem: usageUsed is read once at request start (line 174-211) and each action writes `.update({ aiya_messages_used: usageUsed + 1 })` (lines 368, 463, 494) using that snapshot value. This is a classic lost-update race: if a user fires N requests concurrently (trivial on mobile — double tap, retry, multiple tabs), all read the same usageUsed=k and all write k+1, so the counter advances by 1 instead of N. The limit check at line 213 also uses the stale snapshot. Net effect: the 50-message cap can be blown past arbitrarily and OpenAI spend (gpt-4o at full price) is uncapped under concurrency.
fix: Make the increment atomic and authoritative. Add a Postgres RPC, e.g. `create function increment_aiya_usage(p_user uuid) returns table(used int, limit int) ...` that does `UPDATE users SET aiya_messages_used = aiya_messages_used + 1 WHERE id = p_user AND aiya_messages_used < aiya_messages_limit RETURNING ...`, returning no row when over limit. Call it via supabaseAdmin.rpc; if it returns no row, respond 429. This enforces the cap atomically and counts every billed call.

verdict.reasoning: The race is real and matches the code exactly. usageUsed is read once at lines 174-178 into a local snapshot; the only limit check is the single line-213 `if (usageUsed >= usageLimit)` using that snapshot; and all three counted write sites (lines 368, 463, 494) do `.update({ aiya_messages_used: usageUsed + 1 })` from that same request-start value rather than an atomic DB-side increment (e.g. `aiya_messages_used = aiya_messages_used + 1`). This is a classic lost-update read-modify-write race: N concurrent requests all read used=k and all write k+1, so the counter advances by 1 instead of N. The 50-message cap (migration 20260207010000 sets aiya_messages_limit=50; column is a plain integer) can therefore be exceeded under concurrency, and the extra gpt-4o calls are billed. Mobile double-tap/retry/multi-tab makes this trivially reproducible. Two corrections to the finding's framing: (1) classify (line 311) and category (line 332) actions return early and do NOT increment — only analysis, profile, and the default chat path count usage when countUsage !== false; so the cap governs a subset of OpenAI calls. (2) More importantly, every increment happens AFTER the callOpenAI call, and the only gate is the single pre-flight check at line 213. So an atomic counter alone does NOT prevent a concurrent burst's OpenAI spend — all in-flight requests pass line 213 before anyone increments, fire their OpenAI calls, then increment. The atomic RPC fixes counter corruption and future cap enforcement but, placed after callOpenAI, would still let a concurrent batch leak OpenAI cost. The blast radius is per-user (a user inflating their own counter), not cross-user, which bounds the cost-leak. Severity high is slightly overstated for an abuse/cost concern that is self-limited per user and not a data-exposure/security hole; medium is more accurate, though the unbounded-per-user cost angle keeps it non-trivial.
verdict.refinedFix: The RPC approach is correct and matches existing SECURITY DEFINER conventions in this repo (supabase-fix.sql, 20260207000000_add_aiya_chats.sql). Refinements: (1) Move the atomic check-and-increment to BEFORE callOpenAI for counted actions, not after — otherwise concurrent requests still all pass the line-213 gate and incur OpenAI spend before any counter update. (2) Reserve-then-refund semantics: increment atomically up front; if the request errors out before producing a reply, the increment already happened (acceptable, or add a decrement on failure). Concretely: create function public.increment_aiya_usage(p_user uuid) returns table(used int, lim int) language plpgsql security definer as $$ begin return query update public.users set aiya_messages_used = aiya_messages_used + 1 where id = p_user and aiya_messages_used < aiya_messages_limit returning aiya_messages_used, aiya_messages_limit; end; $$;  Then revoke execute from public/anon/authenticated and grant only to service_role (the edge function uses supabaseAdmin/service role, which bypasses RLS anyway). In index.ts, for the three counted paths gated by `countUsage !== false`, replace the read-at-start check plus post-call .update with: call supabaseAdmin.rpc('increment_aiya_usage', { p_user: userId }); if it returns no row, respond 429 'Usage limit exceeded' and skip the OpenAI call; otherwise proceed and use the returned used/limit in the usage payload. Keep the existing line 174-211 read only to bootstrap the user row (the upsert branch); remove the line-213 stale check since the RPC now enforces the cap atomically. Note the ?? 50 / DEFAULT_LIMIT fallbacks become unnecessary for the counted path since the DB returns authoritative values.

title: 'category' action uses non-normalized comparison while 'classify' uses normalized — category path silently unreachable for non-exact casing
problem: The function normalizes action: `const normalizedAction = String(action||'').toLowerCase().trim()` (line 230) and dispatches classify via `if (normalizedAction === 'classify')` (line 235). But the 'category' branch (line 314) uses `if (action === 'category')` against the RAW action. The comment at line 234 claims normalization is needed because action casing/whitespace can vary, yet 'category' (and 'analysis'/'profile'/chat) ignore that normalization. If a 'category' request ever arrives with stray whitespace or different casing, it falls through every branch to the default chat handler at line 476 — returning a free-form chat reply (gpt-4o, billed) instead of a one-word category, and suggestCategory() in the client will get a malformed response. Inconsistent dispatch is a latent correctness bug.
fix: Use normalizedAction consistently for all branches: `if (normalizedAction === 'category')`, `=== 'analysis'`, `=== 'profile'`, and gate the chat fallback on `normalizedAction === 'chat'`. Either normalize everywhere or nowhere — the current half-normalized dispatch is the bug.

title: First message in a chat can never reach crisis tier (crisis check is unreachable for messageCount 0)
problem: routeMessage returns early for messageCountInChat===0 with tier 'deep' (line 96-98) BEFORE the CRISIS_WORDS check at line 101. So if a user's very first message in a new chat is a crisis disclosure ('intihar etmek istiyorum'), it is routed as 'deep', not 'crisis'. Even once crisis instructions exist (ai-aiya-1), the most common real-world case — someone opening Aiya specifically to disclose — would bypass crisis handling. The first-message branch should not short-circuit the crisis branch.
fix: Move the CRISIS_WORDS check above the messageCountInChat===0 early return, or have the first-message branch fall through to the crisis check first. e.g. `if (CRISIS_WORDS.some(...)) return crisisRoute; if (messageCountInChat === 0) return deepRoute; ...`.

verdict.reasoning:
The factual ordering claim is correct. In src/services/aiyaService.ts, routeMessage returns early at line 96-98 for messageCountInChat===0 with tier 'deep', BEFORE the CRISIS_WORDS check at line 101-103. The caller (src/pages/Aiya.tsx:889-890) sets messageCount = history.length, so a genuinely first message has count 0 and short-circuits to 'deep' — a first-message crisis disclosure like 'intihar etmek istiyorum' is labeled 'deep', never 'crisis'. That part is real.

BUT the 'high' severity and the claimed user impact are overstated, because in the current code the tier label has essentially no behavioral consequence for this case:
1. The 'crisis' RouteResult is byte-for-byte identical to the first-message 'deep' RouteResult: both are { memoryCount: MAX_CONTEXT_MEMORIES, historyLimit: 50, includeStats: true, includeFullPrompt: true, includeProfile: true }. Only the tier string differs.
2. route.tier is consumed in exactly two places: a DEV-only console.log (Aiya.tsx:912) and the charBudget ternary (aiyaService.ts:416-418), where 'crisis' and 'deep' BOTH fall through to the same MAX_CONTEXT_CHARS default branch.
3. route.tier is never sent to the edge function. aiyaService.sendMessage only forwards message/history/memories/locale/systemPrompt/memoryContext (Aiya.tsx:915-919). Grep for crisis|tier in supabase/functions/aiya-chat/index.ts returns no matches.
4. There are NO crisis instructions anywhere in the system prompt (i18n.ts) or edge function — confirming related finding ai-aiya-1. So even when CRISIS_WORDS matches on message 2+, nothing crisis-specific happens today.

Net: a first-message crisis discloser currently receives the EXACT same full-context handling the 'crisis' tier would produce. The defect is a real latent ordering bug and a genuine prerequisite for ai-aiya-1 to ever take effect, but on its own it produces zero observable behavior change. Hence 'partial': the bug exists and the fix is correct, but the stated severity/impact only holds once crisis handling (ai-aiya-1) is actually implemented.

title: length>300 cannot trigger crisis/deep escalation correctly — long crisis messages after first msg routed as 'deep' but never as 'crisis' unless a keyword matches
problem: The router relies entirely on substring keyword matching for crisis/deep detection. A long, paraphrased distress message that avoids the exact CRISIS_WORDS / DEEP_WORDS strings (e.g. describing hopelessness without the literal token 'hopeless'/'çaresiz') falls through to 'normal' tier with only 15 memories and the compact prompt — even at length>300 it only reaches 'deep' (line 106), never crisis. The keyword lists are also brittle: 'can not take it anymore' (line 71) will never match real input which is 'can't take it anymore' or 'cant take it anymore' (apostrophe/spacing differ), so that crisis phrase is effectively dead. 'panik atak' is in DEEP but English 'panic attack' is only partially covered ('anxiety' yes, 'panic' no).
fix: Normalize input (strip/normalize apostrophes and collapse whitespace) before matching, and fix dead entries: replace 'can not take it anymore' with token matches like 'take it anymore' / 'cant take it' / 'can\'t take it'. Add 'panic attack'. Consider matching on word stems rather than full phrases. Longer term, a cheap classifier pass (gpt-4o-mini) for crisis detection would be far more robust than substring lists, but at minimum fix the unmatchable entries.

title: Casual tier strips ALL profile and stats even deep into a conversation, degrading 'knows me' quality
problem: Any short greeting-like message ('naber', 'selam', length<60) at ANY point in a long, emotionally deep conversation routes to 'casual': includeProfile=false, includeStats=false, memoryCount=5, and handleSend swaps to the no-profile compact prompt (Aiya.tsx:905). So after 20 messages of deep sharing, a user typing 'peki' or 'selam' gets a response from a model that has just been stripped of the profile summary and stats it had moments ago — the assistant can feel like it suddenly 'forgot' them, undermining the core differentiator the prompt brags about. The casual optimization ignores conversation depth.
fix: Gate the casual tier on conversation position too — e.g. only allow casual when messageCountInChat is low (say < 4) or when the previous turns were also casual. Once a conversation has reached deep/crisis, keep profile in-context for subsequent short messages. Alternatively always keep the (small) profile summary in the prompt; it is far cheaper than re-establishing rapport.

title: classify falls back to gratitude/personal on any model hiccup — systematically mislabels memories
problem: In the classify branch, category defaults to 'gratitude' and lifeArea to 'personal' (lines 277-278). If safeJsonParse fails or the model returns an unexpected shape, only narrow keyword heuristics (hasFunKeywords/hasSuccessKeywords/hasWorkKeywords, lines 240-243, 292-308) can override the defaults — covering only a handful of categories (no love/peace/inspiration/growth/adventure keyword fallback at all, and lifeArea fallback only flips personal->work). So a memory like 'sevgilimle harika bir akşam' that fails to parse silently becomes gratitude/personal. This produces a persistent bias toward gratitude/personal across the user's memory dataset (which then feeds buildMemoryStats 'TOP EMOTIONS' and the whole analysis), and the system prompt for category even warns 'Do not default to gratitude' (line 317) precisely because this default is known-bad.
fix: When parsing fails, return null / 'uncategorized' rather than guessing gratitude/personal, and let the client treat null as 'leave unset' (the client suggestCategoryAndLifeArea already returns null gracefully on null category). Or retry once. Do not hard-default to the single most over-represented category. Also expand keyword fallback to all 8 categories if you keep heuristics.

title: maybeUpdateProfile passes wrong message array — drops the user's last message and message count is off
problem: After a successful reply, the code calls `maybeUpdateProfile([...history, aiyaMsg])` (line 947). Here `history` (line 886) is the trimmed messages snapshot taken BEFORE the user's current message was appended to chatsRef — it does NOT include the just-sent userMsg, and it appends only the assistant reply. So the profile builder receives history that is missing the most recent user turn, and `count = nextMessages.length` (line 839) used for the PROFILE_UPDATE_MESSAGE_INTERVAL / profileMeta.messageCount bookkeeping is off-by-one/skewed versus the real chat length. The profile — which is injected into every future prompt as Aiya's 'memory' — is thus built from a subtly wrong transcript and the every-5-messages cadence drifts.
fix: Build the array from the authoritative updated chat: read chatsRef.current for targetChatId after the assistant message is committed (or construct `[...history, userMsg, aiyaMsg]` explicitly). Ensure the message used for `count` matches the actual persisted chat length so the interval/cooldown logic is correct.

title: Client throws away the API's usageLimit and hardcodes 50, so a real lower/over-limit server state is invisible to the user
problem: usageInfo deliberately ignores the limit returned by the edge function and forces `limit = 50` (lines 419, 425, 433, with comment 'Always 50, never use API's limit'). This was a stopgap for the old 30->50 migration (supabase/migrations/20260207010000), but it is now a hardcoded business value in the UI that contradicts the server as the source of truth. If the server ever returns 429 'Usage limit exceeded' because the real aiya_messages_limit is something other than 50 (e.g. a future premium tier, or a row still at 30 the migration missed), the UI still shows x/50 and a non-full bar — so the user sees capacity remaining while every send fails. The displayed counter and the actual enforcement diverge.
fix: Use the server-provided usage.limit (fall back to user.aiyaMessagesLimit, then 50 only as last resort). Remove the hardcoded override. The limit belongs to the DB/edge function, not the page. This also future-proofs premium tiers.

title: analysis and profile actions are billed but bypass the gpt-4o-mini cost optimization; analysis uses full gpt-4o on large context
problem: MODEL_MINI (gpt-4o-mini, '16x cheaper input' per the comment at line 16) is used only for category/classify. The 'analysis' (line 350) and 'profile' (line 450) actions both call callOpenAI with no model param, defaulting to full gpt-4o (line 102), while feeding them the entire memoryContext (up to MAX_CONTEXT_CHARS=16000 chars / 80 memories). These are the two largest-input calls in the system and run on the most expensive model. analyzeMemories counts usage (countUsage default true) but buildProfile is called with countUsage:false (aiyaService.ts:701) AND is auto-triggered every 5 messages (Aiya.tsx PROFILE_UPDATE_MESSAGE_INTERVAL=5) — so a recurring, uncounted, full-price gpt-4o call on max context fires silently in the background, invisible to the usage meter and the user.
fix: Evaluate gpt-4o-mini for analysis/profile (these are summarization/extraction tasks mini handles well) to cut cost dramatically, or cap the memoryContext size passed to them. At minimum, make the recurring background profile build count toward usage or rate-limit it server-side, since it is real OpenAI spend that currently escapes the 50-message budget entirely.

title: Stats-header char budget is subtracted from memory budget, silently dropping memories on rich profiles
problem: In buildTieredMemoryContext, totalChars is seeded with statsHeader.length (line 420) and the loop breaks when totalChars exceeds charBudget (line 425). The stats header can be up to STATS_HEADER_BUDGET=2000 chars (line 349). For the 'normal' tier the charBudget is only 8000, so up to 25% of the budget is consumed by the header before any memory line is added, meaning users with dense stats get noticeably fewer actual memory lines than route.memoryCount implies — and the truncation is silent. For deep/crisis the budget is MAX_CONTEXT_CHARS=16000 which is also the hard cap used elsewhere, so the header pushes total context above the intended memory ceiling.
fix: Either budget the stats header separately from the memory budget (compute memory lines against charBudget, then prepend the header), or raise the per-tier budgets to account for the header. Make the intended memory line count actually achievable.

title: Empty-payload / invalid-JSON path increments nothing but the limit check ran on a stale snapshot; classify/category never enforce or consume the limit
problem: classify (line 235) and category (line 314) always call OpenAI (real cost via gpt-4o-mini) but never check or increment usage — they're invoked automatically by the client on memory creation (suggestCategoryAndLifeArea, aiyaService.ts:573, countUsage:false). There is no server-side rate limit on these at all, so a client (or a malicious caller with a valid token) can call classify unboundedly and run up OpenAI spend with zero accounting. The 50-message cap only governs chat/analysis/profile. Combined with finding ai-aiya-2's non-atomic counting, the cost-control story has real holes.
fix: Add a separate, cheap rate limit for classification calls (e.g. a per-minute cap or fold them into a daily classification budget), even if they don't consume the chat quota. At minimum log/meter them so spend is observable.

title: Error body detection requires 'reply'/'category'/'analysis'/'profile' keys — a valid empty/edge response with an 'error'-like field is misclassified
problem: invokeAiya treats any object with an 'error' key and none of reply/category/analysis/profile as a thrown error (line 522). The classify success response is `{category, lifeArea}` — it has 'category', so it's safe. But this guard is fragile: any future action returning a shape without one of those four sentinel keys (e.g. a hypothetical {data:...} or a success object that happens to carry a field named 'error') would be thrown as an error to the user. It couples the generic invoker to a hardcoded whitelist of response shapes that must be kept in sync with every action.
fix: Have the edge function include an explicit success/ok discriminator (e.g. always return {ok:true,...} on success and {ok:false,error} on failure) and key the client check on that, instead of inferring failure from the absence of specific success keys.

title: aiya_chats.user_id has no foreign key to users — orphan rows on account deletion
problem: The aiya_chats table declares user_id as "uuid" NOT NULL but defines NO foreign key constraint referencing public.users(id). Every other user-scoped table (memories, connections, ai_analyses, weekly_summaries, daily_question_answers) has a FK with ON DELETE CASCADE to public.users. Because aiya_chats lacks this, when a user (and their public.users row / auth.users row) is deleted, all of that user's aiya_chats rows are left behind as orphans forever. They are also unreachable (RLS auth.uid() = user_id never matches a deleted user) but still consume storage and leak conversation content that should have been removed on account deletion (GDPR/privacy concern, given privacy-policy.html was just added for Play Store).
fix: Add a foreign key in a new migration: ALTER TABLE public.aiya_chats ADD CONSTRAINT aiya_chats_user_id_fkey FOREIGN KEY (user_id) REFERENCES public.users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE; (Pre-clean any existing orphan rows first: DELETE FROM public.aiya_chats WHERE user_id NOT IN (SELECT id FROM public.users);)

verdict.reasoning: Confirmed by reading the actual code. supabase/migrations/20260207000000_add_aiya_chats.sql lines 5-13 declare aiya_chats with `user_id uuid NOT NULL` and only a PRIMARY KEY on id — NO foreign key to public.users. Every other user-scoped table DOES have `FOREIGN KEY (user_id) REFERENCES public.users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE`: ai_analyses, connections, memories, weekly_summaries (20251220174815_remote_schema.sql:191/196/201/211) and daily_question_answers (20260206100000_memory_system_overhaul.sql:90). public.users.id itself cascades from auth.users (line 206). Critically, the account-deletion handler in src/components/SettingsSheet.tsx:261-312 (handleDeleteAccount) explicitly deletes only `memories` then `users`, relying on FK cascade for all other child tables. Because aiya_chats has no FK, its rows are NOT deleted on account deletion — they orphan permanently. The deletion confirmation text (i18n key deleteAccountConfirm) promises "All your data will be deleted," and aiya_chats.messages stores full conversation content as jsonb, so this is a real data-retention/privacy (GDPR) gap, reinforced by the just-added privacy-policy.html. Orphans are unreachable (RLS auth.uid()=user_id never matches a deleted user, and auth won't reissue the uuid), so there is NO cross-user exposure — only residual storage of content that should have been purged. FK target is valid: users_pkey PRIMARY KEY(id), and uuid types match.
verdict.refinedFix:
Add a new migration named to sort after the latest existing one (20260228000000), e.g. supabase/migrations/20260301000000_add_aiya_chats_user_fk.sql:

-- Remove any orphan rows first so the constraint can be added
DELETE FROM public.aiya_chats WHERE user_id NOT IN (SELECT id FROM public.users);

-- Add FK matching the pattern used by every other user-scoped table
ALTER TABLE public.aiya_chats
  ADD CONSTRAINT aiya_chats_user_id_fkey
  FOREIGN KEY (user_id) REFERENCES public.users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE;

Notes: user_id is NOT NULL so the NOT IN cleanup is NULL-safe. Optionally also add an explicit `await supabase.from('aiya_chats').delete().eq('user_id', user.id)` in handleDeleteAccount before the users delete, for defense-in-depth and to clean existing production orphans, but the FK cascade alone fixes future deletions. The DELETE pre-clean must run before the ALTER (as the proposed fix states) or the constraint addition fails on existing orphans.

title: SupabaseMemoryRow type omits the categories column (schema drift)
problem: Migration 20260228000000 adds a real categories TEXT[] column to memories, and memoryService reads/writes it (mapMemoryToSupabase sends categories, the incremental select on line 330 fetches categories, mapSupabaseToMemory maps it). But the exported SupabaseMemoryRow interface in src/types/supabase.ts has NO categories field. The interface is documented (line 38) as the canonical Supabase memories row shape and references memoryMapper.ts, yet memoryMapper.ts is a 1-line stub (the warning shows it has 1 line) and no longer defines SupabaseMemoryRow. So the only typed representation of a memories row is stale relative to the DB. Any code that types a row as SupabaseMemoryRow loses categories at compile time.
fix: Add `categories?: string[]` to SupabaseMemoryRow in src/types/supabase.ts, and either restore the SupabaseMemoryRow definition referenced in memoryMapper.ts or update the doc comment to stop pointing at the empty mapper file.

title: Memory date shifts back one day in negative-UTC timezones on read-back
problem: On write, the date is stored as a bare YYYY-MM-DD string (line 17: .split('T')[0]) into a Postgres `date` column. On read-back, mapSupabaseToMemory does `new Date(row.date).toISOString()` (line 50). `new Date('2026-06-20')` parses a date-only string as UTC midnight; calling toISOString() keeps it at 2026-06-20T00:00:00Z, but when that ISO value is later rendered with the user's local timezone (anything west of UTC, e.g. Americas), it displays as 2026-06-19. A memory saved on the 20th appears on the 19th after a cloud pull. This is a silent correctness bug that only manifests for negative-offset users, so it can pass Turkey-based testing (UTC+3) unnoticed.
fix: Treat the date as a calendar date, not an instant. Either keep it as the raw YYYY-MM-DD string (drop the new Date(...).toISOString() round-trip and store date as 'YYYY-MM-DD'), or construct it timezone-safely, e.g. `new Date(row.date + 'T00:00:00').toISOString()` is still wrong for display; preferred fix is to stop converting and keep Memory.date as the YYYY-MM-DD string consistently with what is written on line 17.

verdict.reasoning:
The underlying symptom is REAL and reproducible, but the finding mislocates the root cause and its proposed fix does not work.

WRITE PATH: MemoryForm uses <input type="date"> which yields a bare 'YYYY-MM-DD' string (MemoryForm.tsx:1142). On submit, date: formData.date is passed unchanged (MemoryForm.tsx:501/517) to memoryService.create, so the LOCAL Memory.date is already 'YYYY-MM-DD'. mapMemoryToSupabase line 17 .split('T')[0] stores 'YYYY-MM-DD' into the Postgres date column. Correct.

READ PATH: mapSupabaseToMemory line 50 does new Date(row.date).toISOString(). row.date is '2026-06-20', new Date() parses date-only as UTC midnight, so toISOString() yields '2026-06-20T00:00:00.000Z'. Verified by running node.

DISPLAY: Sites such as Home.tsx:585 and :845, exportService.ts:91/129, Connections.tsx:210, Achievements all do new Date(memory.date).toLocaleDateString(locale) with NO timeZone:'UTC' option, i.e. they render in the user's local timezone. I reproduced: stored '2026-06-20T00:00:00.000Z' displays as 6/19/2026 in America/New_York and 6/20/2026 in Europe/Istanbul. So the off-by-one for negative-UTC users is confirmed and would pass UTC+3 Turkey testing.

WHY THE FIX IS WRONG: The proposed fix is 'drop the new Date(...).toISOString() round-trip and keep Memory.date as YYYY-MM-DD'. But I ran node on the bare string too: new Date('2026-06-20').toLocaleDateString in America/New_York ALSO yields 6/19/2026. The display sites call new Date(memory.date), which parses a date-only string as UTC midnight regardless of whether the stored value is the bare string or the ISO instant. So removing line 50's round-trip changes nothing the user sees — the bug lives at the render layer (new Date(bareDate).toLocaleDateString in local TZ), not at line 50. Line 50 is a code smell (turning a calendar date into a UTC instant) and makes representation inconsistent with line 17, but it is NOT the cause of the visible shift, and fixing only it does not fix the symptom.

Severity: the original 'high' overstates a service-layer round-trip bug; the actual user-visible defect is a consistent one-day display shift for all negative-UTC users across many screens and exports. That is a genuine correctness issue but cosmetic (no data corruption — the stored value is correct), so medium is more accurate.
verdict.refinedFix:
Fix at the render layer, not just line 50. Two coordinated changes:

1) Normalize storage to a bare calendar date. In mapSupabaseToMemory (memoryService.ts:50) replace:
   date: new Date(row.date).toISOString(),
with:
   date: String(row.date).split('T')[0],
This keeps Memory.date consistently 'YYYY-MM-DD' (matching the local write path and line 17), avoiding the UTC-instant detour. This alone does NOT fix display.

2) Make all date displays parse the calendar date in local time, not UTC. Add a shared util in src/utils (e.g. formatMemoryDate(dateStr, locale, opts)) that parses 'YYYY-MM-DD' to a LOCAL-midnight Date:
   const [y, m, d] = dateStr.split('T')[0].split('-').map(Number)
   const dt = new Date(y, (m||1) - 1, d || 1)
   return dt.toLocaleDateString(locale, opts)
Then replace the new Date(memory.date).toLocaleDateString(...) call sites: Home.tsx:585 and :845, exportService.ts:91 and :129, Connections.tsx:210 (lastUsed), and review Statistics.tsx:145 / useMemoryFilters.ts:77,87 / aiyaService.ts comparisons for the same UTC-midnight parsing pitfall (comparisons of bare dates vs new Date() can also be off by a day in negative-UTC). 

Simplest equivalent alternative for display-only sites: pass { timeZone: 'UTC', ...existingOpts } to toLocaleDateString, which cancels the UTC-midnight shift. Either approach is non-breaking; the local-calendar-parse util is preferred for consistency. Verify build (npm run build) and add a unit test that mocks a negative-UTC offset.

title: users INSERT RLS policy uses WITH CHECK (true) — any authenticated user can insert arbitrary user rows
problem: The policy `"Users can insert own data" ON public.users FOR INSERT WITH CHECK (true)` allows ANY caller (anon or authenticated, both are granted INSERT via the GRANT ALL on lines 485-487) to insert a public.users row with ANY id and ANY email — it does not enforce auth.uid() = id. While the FK users_id_fkey -> auth.users(id) blocks inserting an id that has no matching auth user, an authenticated user could still insert a row for a DIFFERENT existing auth user id (e.g. set is_premium=true for someone, or squat an email), or insert their own row with a forged email different from their auth email. The matching UPDATE/SELECT policies correctly use auth.uid() = id; only INSERT is open.
fix: Tighten the policy: DROP POLICY "Users can insert own data" ON public.users; CREATE POLICY "Users can insert own data" ON public.users FOR INSERT WITH CHECK (auth.uid() = id); The app's ensureUserExists (src/lib/userService.ts:114) always inserts with id = the authenticated user's own id, so this will not break the normal signup path.

title: categories[] array values are not validated by any CHECK constraint
problem: The memories_category_check constraint only validates the scalar `category` column against the allowed enum. The categories TEXT[] column (the field the app now treats as the source of truth per Memory type comment in src/types/index.ts:8-9) has NO constraint at all — its default is ARRAY['uncategorized'] but any string array can be written. memoryService update (line 264) forwards updates.categories verbatim to Supabase with no server-side validation, so a stale client or malformed payload can persist categories like ['xyz'] that the MemoryCategory union type forbids. mapSupabaseToMemory then casts row.categories straight to Memory['categories'] (memoryService line 48) with no runtime check, propagating invalid values back into the app.
fix: Add a CHECK constraint validating array contents, e.g.: ALTER TABLE memories ADD CONSTRAINT memories_categories_check CHECK (categories <@ ARRAY['uncategorized','success','peace','fun','love','gratitude','inspiration','growth','adventure']::text[]); (the <@ "is contained by" operator validates every element).

title: No index on memories.updated_at despite incremental sync filtering and ordering by it
problem: The incremental sync query (the hottest read path, run on every poll) does `.select(...).eq('user_id', userId).order('updated_at', { ascending: false })` and `.gt('updated_at', lastSyncedAt)` (memoryService lines 332,335). The migration creates indexes on user_id, category, date, and life_area but NOT on updated_at. As memory counts grow, every incremental poll forces Postgres to filter+sort by updated_at without index support. A composite (user_id, updated_at) index would let the gt-filter and ordering be served directly, reducing egress/CPU on the polling path the codebase explicitly optimized for cost.
fix: Add: CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS memories_user_id_updated_at_idx ON public.memories (user_id, updated_at DESC); This supersedes the standalone memories_user_id_idx for these queries.

title: No index on categories array despite category being a primary filter dimension
problem: The legacy scalar category column has a btree index (memories_category_idx, line 174), but the new categories TEXT[] column — which src/types/index.ts:8-9 designates as the new source of truth replacing the deprecated scalar — has no index. Any server-side filtering by category membership (e.g. categories @> ARRAY['love']) would do a sequential scan. If category filtering is currently done only client-side this is low impact, but the scalar index is now partly dead weight while the live column is unindexed.
fix: If/when filtering categories server-side, add a GIN index: CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS memories_categories_gin_idx ON public.memories USING gin (categories); Otherwise consider dropping the now-deprecated memories_category_idx to avoid maintaining a dead index.

title: weekly_summaries allows duplicate rows per user per week (no UNIQUE constraint, no index)
problem: weekly_summaries has only a primary key on id. There is no UNIQUE (user_id, week_start) constraint and no index on user_id (unlike connections/memories which have user_id indexes). Nothing prevents inserting two summaries for the same user and same week, and lookups by user_id do a sequential scan. connections by contrast correctly has connections_user_id_name_key UNIQUE (user_id, name) plus connections_user_id_idx — weekly_summaries is missing both equivalents.
fix: Add: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS weekly_summaries_user_week_key ON public.weekly_summaries (user_id, week_start); (a unique index also serves as the user_id lookup index). Use upsert with onConflict on (user_id, week_start) when writing summaries.

title: users.aiya_messages_limit DEFAULT is still 30 while app and migration use 50
problem: The column default for aiya_messages_limit is still 30 (remote_schema line 113). Migration 20260207010000 only UPDATEs existing rows to 50 (a one-time data fix) and does NOT change the column DEFAULT. So any new public.users row created WITHOUT an explicit aiya_messages_limit gets 30. The app's ensureUserExists happens to pass 50 explicitly (userService line 122), masking this, but any row created by another path (a DB trigger, manual insert, or future code that omits the field) would silently get the wrong 30 limit. The mapper default is also 50 (userMapper line 16), so the DB default is the lone inconsistent value.
fix: In a migration, align the column default: ALTER TABLE public.users ALTER COLUMN aiya_messages_limit SET DEFAULT 50;

title: daily_question_answers.is_public=true rows are globally readable but never restricted by a public flag on the table's other fields — and there is no UPDATE/DELETE policy
problem: The policy "Anyone can read public answers" exposes the FULL row (including user_id and the linked memory_id) of any answer where is_public = true to every authenticated user. There is no column-level restriction, so making an answer public also exposes the author's user_id and the memory_id linkage. Additionally there is no UPDATE or DELETE policy on daily_question_answers, so a user can never un-publish or delete their own answer once written (RLS denies by default). Given the comment calls public answers a "Future" feature, shipping the open SELECT policy now is premature exposure.
fix: Either remove the "Anyone can read public answers" policy until the feature is built, or restrict exposed columns via a view. Also add UPDATE/DELETE policies: CREATE POLICY "Users can update own answers" ON public.daily_question_answers FOR UPDATE USING (auth.uid() = user_id) WITH CHECK (auth.uid() = user_id); and the equivalent FOR DELETE.

title: users SELECT policy blocks reading other users' public profile data, but avatar/displayName columns were added for social-style profiles
problem: Migration 20260206050000 adds display_name, bio, avatar_url, birthday, location to users — fields that read like a public/shareable profile. But the only SELECT policy on users is "Users can view own data" USING (auth.uid() = id), so a user can only ever read their OWN row. If any current or planned feature shows another user's name/avatar (e.g. public daily-question answers from finding db-schema-10, which expose user_id), the join to users will return nothing under RLS, silently rendering empty profiles. This is a latent mismatch between the profile-field migration intent and the RLS model.
fix: Confirm whether cross-user profile display is intended. If yes, add a narrowly scoped policy/view exposing only display_name + avatar_url (never email/bio/birthday/location) for authenticated users. If no, document that profile fields are private-only so future devs don't assume they are visible to others.

title: mapSupabaseToMemory casts DB strings to enum types with no runtime validation, allowing constraint drift to corrupt app state
problem: mapSupabaseToMemory blindly casts row.category as Memory['category'] and row.life_area as Memory['lifeArea'] (lines 47,52). The DB CHECK constraints and the TypeScript MemoryCategory/LifeArea unions are maintained in two places and have already diverged historically (category enum was expanded across 3 separate migrations: 20251221, 20260206100000, 20260228000000). If a future migration adds a DB value not present in the union (or vice-versa), the cast hides it and the value flows into the app where exhaustive switch/UI mapping may not handle it, producing blank UI rather than a clear error.
fix: Validate against a single source of truth: keep the allowed-values arrays in one TS const, derive both the union type and a runtime guard from it, and in mapSupabaseToMemory fall back to 'uncategorized' when row.category/life_area is not in the allowed set (mirroring the existing 'uncategorized' fallback already used for life_area on line 52).

title: Destructive ConfirmationDialog has no Escape key, focus trap, or scroll lock
problem: ConfirmationDialog is the primary confirm surface for destructive actions (delete memory, bulk delete, delete account, logout, delete Aiya chat). Unlike ModalShell it registers no keydown handler, so Escape does NOT close it; it does not trap focus (Tab leaks to the page behind the backdrop, and screen-reader/keyboard users can interact with obscured content); and it does not lock body scroll, so the page behind scrolls on wheel/touch. This is the most-used modal in the app and the one where accidental focus on background controls is most dangerous.
fix: Reuse ModalShell as the container for ConfirmationDialog (it already provides Escape, focus trap, focus restore, and useBodyScrollLock), or replicate ModalShell's useEffect that adds a window 'keydown' Escape->onClose listener, the Tab focus-trap, and call useBodyScrollLock(isOpen). At minimum add the Escape handler and useBodyScrollLock(isOpen).

verdict.reasoning:
Re-read src/components/ConfirmationDialog.tsx (full file, 1-129) and confirmed all three gaps are real:

1. ESCAPE: There is no useEffect and no window 'keydown' listener anywhere in the component. A repo-wide grep for keydown/Escape returns only ModalShell.tsx and ImageModal.tsx, so there is no global handler either. Escape genuinely does NOT close ConfirmationDialog. ModalShell.tsx:101-109 has exactly this handler, confirming the asymmetry the finding describes.

2. FOCUS TRAP / RESTORE: ConfirmationDialog has no panelRef, no focusable-node collection, no previouslyFocusedRef. Tab leaks to the page behind the backdrop and focus is not restored on close. ModalShell.tsx:111-170 implements both; ConfirmationDialog implements neither.

3. BODY SCROLL LOCK: ConfirmationDialog calls useModalPresence(isOpen) (line 29) but NOT useBodyScrollLock. I read useModalPresence.ts — it only increments/decrements a Zustand modal counter used by Layout for the bottom nav; it never touches document.body/documentElement overflow. So background scroll is genuinely not locked. ModalShell.tsx:95 calls useBodyScrollLock(isOpen); useBodyScrollLock.ts confirms that is the hook that sets overflow:hidden (and position:fixed on iOS).

Usage sites verified as destructive-confirm surfaces (real src, not worktrees): src/pages/Connections.tsx:298 (delete connection, type danger), src/pages/Aiya.tsx:1398 (delete chat, irreversible, type danger), src/pages/Vault.tsx:271 (memory delete/bulk via confirmDialogProps), src/components/SettingsSheet.tsx:812 (account/logout actions), src/components/MemoryForm.tsx:1219. So the "most-used destructive modal" claim holds.

The finding is accurate on facts. I adjusted severity down from high to medium: these are genuine WCAG issues (2.1.2 no-keyboard-trap-escape, 2.4.3 focus order, background-scroll) on a destructive dialog, but no data-loss/security path exists — the destructive action still requires an explicit click on the Confirm button, so a focus leak alone cannot trigger deletion. It is a real accessibility/UX defect worth fixing, not a critical/high production-breaking bug.

Fix safety note: the MINIMAL fix (add an Escape keydown useEffect gated on isOpen + onClose, and call useBodyScrollLock(isOpen)) is correct and non-breaking. The finding's primary suggestion to "reuse ModalShell as the container" is NOT a drop-in: ModalShell renders a mobile bottom-sheet (items-end, full-width, rounded-t-3xl, forced pixel height via VisualViewport, separate header/footer/scroll slots), which would materially change ConfirmationDialog's centered-card design and require restructuring its JSX. So I confirm the finding but recommend the replicate-the-logic variant, not the swap-in-ModalShell variant.
verdict.refinedFix:
Do NOT swap in ModalShell (it is a mobile bottom-sheet with forced height and would change the visual design). Instead add the three behaviors inline to ConfirmationDialog:

1) Scroll lock + Escape (top of component, after useModalPresence(isOpen)):
   import { useEffect, useRef } from 'react'
   import { useBodyScrollLock } from '../hooks/useBodyScrollLock'
   ...
   useBodyScrollLock(isOpen)
   useEffect(() => {
     if (!isOpen) return
     const onKeyDown = (e: KeyboardEvent) => { if (e.key === 'Escape') onClose() }
     window.addEventListener('keydown', onKeyDown)
     return () => window.removeEventListener('keydown', onKeyDown)
   }, [isOpen, onClose])

2) Focus trap + restore (mirror ModalShell.tsx:111-170): add a panelRef on the inner motion.div (line 58-64), give it tabIndex={-1} role="dialog" aria-modal="true", and add the same getFocusable/Tab-trap useEffect plus previouslyFocusedRef capture-on-open / restore-on-cleanup. This is the only non-trivial part; copy ModalShell's implementation verbatim, swapping its panelRef target.

If touching the focus-trap is considered too large, the at-minimum subset (Escape handler + useBodyScrollLock(isOpen)) is fully safe and non-breaking on its own and resolves the two highest-impact gaps. Both onClose and isOpen are already stable props passed in by all five call sites, so the effect deps are correct.

title: ActionSheet, SettingsSheet, EditProfileSheet & ConflictResolutionDialog lack Escape-to-close and focus trap
problem: A grep for keydown/Escape handlers shows only ModalShell.tsx and ImageModal.tsx implement them. These four bottom-sheets/dialogs render fixed overlays but provide no Escape-to-close and no focus trap, so keyboard/AT users can Tab into the obscured page behind the backdrop and cannot dismiss with Escape. SettingsSheet and EditProfileSheet also have no role="dialog"/aria-modal on the panel. This is inconsistent with ModalShell and degrades accessibility for the settings/profile/conflict flows.
fix: Either migrate these to ModalShell (preferred — gives Escape + focus trap + scroll lock + aria-modal for free) or add the same window keydown Escape->onClose effect plus a focus trap to each panel, and add role="dialog" aria-modal="true" to the panel elements.

title: SettingsSheet & EditProfileSheet set body overflow directly, bypassing iOS-safe scroll lock
problem: Both sheets do `document.body.style.overflow = 'hidden'` in a useEffect and reset to '' on unmount. The project already has useBodyScrollLock (src/hooks/useBodyScrollLock.ts) which on native iOS additionally applies position:fixed + top offset to stop background rubber-band scrolling and restores scroll position. By bypassing it, these full-height sheets allow the background to bounce/scroll behind them on iOS, and resetting overflow to '' (rather than the previous value) can clobber a lock held by another simultaneously-open modal (e.g. the nested ConfirmationDialog inside SettingsSheet).
fix: Replace the manual body.style.overflow effect in both components with `useBodyScrollLock(true)` (the hook is already imported elsewhere). This restores correct iOS behavior and proper save/restore of the previous overflow value.

title: Login forgot-password modal has no scroll lock, focus trap, or Escape handler
problem: The forgot-password modal is a hand-rolled fixed overlay (motion.div with onClick backdrop dismiss). It has no body scroll lock (background scrolls), no Escape-to-close (only backdrop click), no focus trap, and no role="dialog"/aria-modal. It does autoFocus the email input, but keyboard users cannot dismiss with Escape and can Tab back to the obscured login form.
